utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please be so kind to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Mundis, we still owe you a decision, but I'd first like to have -- but before doing so, we would like to turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see on my screen we are in open session again. Mr. Mundis, is the Prosecution ready to call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Prosecution calls Mr. Habib Trto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Good morning, Mr. Trto, I assume. Do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trto, before I will ask you to make a solemn declaration, I first of all inform you that the Chamber has just given a decision that the protective measures you asked for, that is, facial distortion, are granted. So your face cannot be seen from the outside world. Mr. Trto, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth at the beginning of your testimony. The text of this declaration will now be handed out to you by the usher and I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. Trto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the record, witness, can you please state your full name and your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: My name is Habib Trto and I was born on the 25th of April, 1966 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trto, from the time of your birth to the present, have you continued to live in the city of Sarajevo? I am not sure if that answer was audible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't hear any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is not working very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please assist in putting the microphone a put further to the witness. I heard the witness say "da," which by now we all understand means "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It is true that you have lived in Sarajevo your whole life; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes, thank God.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Trto, do you recall the approximate month and year or date on which the war began in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: The war began in 1992, in early March, because that is when some people started walking around with rifles and I think if you see somebody walking around your house with a rifle, that his intentions are likely not to be very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When the war began, what was your employment status? Were you working at the time and, if so, how were you employed?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes. I worked as a tram driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you continue to work as a tram driver throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: No, not throughout the war. When the shelling of Sarajevo began, I think that the first company that came under fire was the city public transport so that the most of the trams were destroyed, were decimated, and people were let off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time the war began, Mr. Trto, were you married?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was your wife's name?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Edina Trto.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at the time the war began, how long had you been married?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. We didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do understand it is not easy for you, Mr. Trto, but could you please try to speak louder because the interpreters have to hear you and translate it into a language we understand. So if it would be possible to speak a bit louder, it would be highly appreciated. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Trto, at the time the war began, how long had you been married?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Four or five years. Five years, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you and your wife have any children?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would like to turn your attention to September of 1993. During that month, where were you living in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: We lived in Klara Zetkin Street. I think the number was 11 or 13, I think. I can't remember exactly, but that is in Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the summer and early fall of 1993, did your wife regularly visit her mother in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes, she would visit her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where was your mother-in-law living at that time, in what part of the city?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Quite near to where we lived, maybe a few kilometres. The name is Dolac Malta. And the name of the street, I think it was Ivana Krndelja Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when your wife would go and visit her mother, how would she get there?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: In most cases, she went with me. I escorted her myself, my wife and my child would go there. But on that day I was not there, so she went there alone with the child.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say that you escorted her, she did she usually go on foot, that is, she would walk to her mother's?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: It was the safest way to get around the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At that time in the summer and early fall of 1993, were you aware of incidents involving sniper shooting at civilians in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes, there was shooting all over the city. You could not walk around normally. You had to avoid the main intersections, and every street that had a line of sight to the hills, it was not safe. You could not go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time in 1993 when your wife was shot by a sniper?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall a date of that incident?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes, the 26th of September, between 11.00 and 12.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to that day, 26 September, 1993. Do you remember what you were doing that day from the time you first woke up in the morning?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Since I was subject to military obligation, I was a conscript and there was a state of war not only in Sarajevo but in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina and everybody was able to carry rifle -- I don't mean a rifle per se, but able to bear arms were conscripts. And I was in the army; I was a courier and I was carrying the mail to the command, and I had an opportunity to visit my house. I sat down with my wife and the phone rang at one point. It was her mother. She spoke to her and they agreed that they would meet at the Cengic Vila. They did meet there. I went back and she went to Cengic Vila to meet with her mother. And then at around noon I was notified that my wife had been injured. And I said, well, thank God, she is only injured. So I went to my wife's mother. But at first she didn't know herself what had happened. She just knew that shots had been fired and that she was hit by a sniper. She didn't know whether she was alive or just wounded perhaps. I went there. There was a first aid point, I don't know what else to call it, maybe 50 metres away from that place, and I asked what had happened. They told me that they had taken her to the emergency room. And then I asked myself why to the emergency, why not the hospital, because usually only the dead bodies are taken to the emergency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time your wife was shot, were any other people with her, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: There was my child. When my wife was hit, she was holding my daughter by her hand and her mother was there too. Unfortunately, she is not -- she is not alive any more. She died in 1996. She just couldn't take it any more. She couldn't go on living.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "she died in 1996," are you referring to your mother-in-law or to your daughter?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: My mother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trto, after learning that your wife had been taken to the emergency, as you have described it, did you in fact go to the emergency yourself?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what did you discover upon arriving at the emergency?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: These were actually the basements of the emergency ward and that probably used to be garages before the war. There were quite a few dead bodies there. I was not really interested in them. I went from room to room trying to find my wife. Unfortunately, I found her. She was lying there in a corner on a metal gurney. It was a table of sorts. I don't know what it was used before. She was lying there, she had two wounds. Both of them were to her arm. One of the wound was such that the bullet struck her arm and went straight through her heart, so that probably caused her death. I am not a medical expert, but that would be a reasonable explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would like the witness to be shown the documents which have been marked P1675 and P1673.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please assist Mr. Mundis, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trto, I would like you to turn first to the document that is marked P1675 in the upper right-hand corner. I would ask you to take a look through that document and tell us if there are pages in that document that you have seen before.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is and what the various pages in this document consist of, please.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: This page, the first page, I didn't see the description of the events and so I never saw this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "this page," Mr. Trto, if you could specify what page you are referring by the numbers that are stamped on the page, perhaps the last two numbers of the document, which page you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay, let's turn to page null 5. Have you seen that page before, that document?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question. Some of these documents I see for the first time, with the exception of the document 08, 09 and document 11. These documents, I saw for the first time during the preparation for the testimony because, before that, I never saw these documents. These are some police reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me turn your attention then to pages 08 and 09. You have seen these pages before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what is the document that bears the number 08 and 09?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: This document is a death certificate for my deceased wife, and I asked for this document to be issued because I needed some papers for my child, since she had to receive a sort of payment of 50 marks as compensation. So this is the reason why I asked to be issued with this certificate. I went to the emergency ward in order to get this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the date, or perhaps on the form itself you will see the date when you actually requested this death certificate?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness to come closer to the microphone or could we perhaps approach the microphones closer to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher could you...

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes, here we can read that it was issued on the 23rd of March 1993. See, in Sarajevo, and maybe everywhere else in the world, the way we proceed is the following: You need to issue these certificates or you have to report the death to the competent organ in due time. I didn't know that there is a delay. So when I asked for this death certificate to be issued at the municipality in the town house, I had to bring a certificate that my wife was indeed dead. And then I gave that certificate to the town house, and then I had to wait for a decision to be rendered by the police station. So it's a sort of paper issued to me by the police station which would enable me to get a death certificate, the excerpt from the registry of the dead. So it is a very complicated procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if you turn to page 09 and look in box 16 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, before you continue, may I ask you one question. Of course, as you understand, the Chamber tries to read the translation as well. What I see on page with ERN number 08 in the translation, that is not the last one, but the one before, the translation ends at number 14. Then it says there's no page 0026-9009. It seems to me that you are now turning to that very page which is not translated, as far as I can see, unless I overlooked a translation. I am specifically dealing with -- well, let's say on 09, it continues with number 15 where 08 ends with 14. And I think the witness is explaining what might be the date of issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is on page 09, but I don't see a translation for 09. Do you have a translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, we don't, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is able to detect this in approximately 30 seconds. Wouldn't it have been proper for the Prosecution to check after the experience of the last couple of weeks, at least to check every single document you are presenting. There is a whole page missing. It is not a detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it is a matter of translation so if you have any questions in respect of page 09, would you please first ask the witness to read what it is about, if you are questioning him about. I do understand that all the members of the Defence team, the General Galic included, can read page 09 so it might be solved by providing us with a proper translation soon. So, please proceed. But you can't imagine that this doesn't make us very happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you are very kind, but this is a technical document in the Serbian language and your humble servant does not have a transparent access to it, this is an issue I wanted to raise, but it was already raised, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trto, if you could turn the block number 16 on page 09.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please read the first two words next to the number 16.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: It is written "cause of death."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you then look to the box below that where the date is specified? Can you read what that says, please.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: It is written "In Sarajevo -- underneath we have the date 23rd/03/1994 and there is a signature of a doctor. It is a medical doctor called Popovic or Dizparevic. I don't really see the name clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would that be the approximate date that you approached the authorities for the issuance of this death certificate?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I ask you now if you can turn to page 11 of this document, and can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber what this page is.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: This page contains a statement. I declared in the statement that my wife was killed and that she was buried at the Alfakovac cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, if you could, Mr. Trto, I would ask you to turn to page 6 of this document, page 06. If you could now compare page 06 of P1675 with the document, the other document that is before you, P1673. Do these documents appear to be the same document with P1673 being more legible than the page marked 06?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I think so that. It is the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The usher can retrieve the documents from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Trto, at the time of her death, how old was your wife?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: My wife was born on or in 1968, so she was 24 years old. At the time, 25, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trto.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask if the Defence is ready to cross-examine the witness. You will now be examined, Mr. Trto by counsel for the defence. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Trto, good morning?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that on the 18th of November, 1995, you gave a statement to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: What date?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Believe me when I tell you that I really cannot remember the dates correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I show you a document bearing your signature, would you then be able to confirm the date?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I am looking for the statement in the English language. Mr. Trto, the usher will show you a statement. Would you be able to confirm to us if this statement bears your signature, and if the date on which you gave the statement is the correct date? The statement is in the English language.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Trto, you told us today in answering a question put to you by my learned friend that, according to you, the war in Sarajevo began in the month of March of 1992.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The cause of this conflict, was it preceded by some events that in some way punctuated the events that would follow?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I really don't know. To be very honest with you, I do not follow the media. I only know that my neighbours and some other people were carrying weapons. There were barricades erected all over town. There were men with hats and they were saying that they were Serbs, whereas I consider that this is not a Serb army. I don't even know how to tell you. It is our own local Serbs. And if you want to call them Serbs, I would make a mistake. I couldn't call them Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that in the month of March, in the city, and more precisely in the part of the city where you lived in 1992, that there were barricades which, according to you, were erected by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Would you please be kind enough not to call them Serbs, but "them." They were not Serbs. You cannot call them Serbs, these people. Because in Sarajevo, there were Serbs who lived throughout the whole war. Do you understand what I am telling you?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any barricades in Sarajevo erected by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I really didn't hear about that. It is quite possible that there were some, but I didn't know about it. I was not really interested by that fact. I was more taking care of my family and I was working.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if on the 1st of March in Bascarsija, a Serbian guest was at a wedding, was killed, and that was the cause, the initial cause of the conflict that escalated later on in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I really don't know how to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were a conscript, so you were a member of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when did you become a member of the army of BH?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Well, I was a tram driver and then I couldn't really tell you the exact date but sometime around -- I don't know, maybe early -- at the very beginning, it was -- actually, it was part of the Territorial Defence. It wasn't even a Territorial Defence, if you wish, because they were looking for people within the local communes and they were looking to create some formations. I lived to Sokolovic Kolonija, and that was shelled in April. But I can't really tell you the exact date of the event in question. For me, it was something quite new or, rather, in life, I had no idea what a shell was and then all of a sudden I was hearing it and the whole house was shaking. We were -- we lived in Sokolovic Kolonija. We walked there and there a big construction machine on that road, and I can't really remember what day it was but it was the day of the shelling and there were a great deal of soldiers there. There were members of the JNA, reserve members, and nobody could say that they were not reserve soldiers because there was a tank there. And then I was driving the tram and I couldn't really go back. I wanted to go back, but I was not able to go back. They called me --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And this is when you moved?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the part of town called Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: First I went to live at my sister's. She lives in Dolac Malta. And from there because the wife of my wife, my mother-in-law, was in 1992 chased away from Grbavica. First she was expelled and then, at the beginning of 1993, her father was also expelled from Grbavica, and we all lived in one apartment. We were six or seven living in one apartment. You know how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did you become a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: It wasn't really the Territorial Defence per se. I don't really know how to call it. In June, probably, when really everybody had to join. There was no other way to stay alive, to have food or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So then up until the month of June of 1992, you were a driver; you were employed as such?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: In the month of May, I think, I can't really tell you the precise date. But in May they started to shoot on tramways in Skenderija, and after that moment, the tramways were no longer operational. They were burning tramways.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that there was a tramway that was set on fire in Skenderija, was that the consequence of a paramilitary formation attack? Members of the units of Juka Prazina and the green berets, when they attacked the caserne, or the barracks actually, when members of the JNA were killed, is this when the setting on the tramway on fire occurred?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I am just asking you if you know if that is linked to that event, is that the same event, say yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I watched it on TV, I wasn't present. Do you understand me? I do not know who was killed there. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I am only asking you if you know that that was that incident. If you do not know, you don't have to answer.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I really don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you became a member of the Territorial Defence, where did you report, to which headquarters of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: It was not the headquarters of the Territorial Defence, it was just a local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: On Malta.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us on what street, and was it inside the building where people lived? Was it an apartment building or was it an office building?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were a courier?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what military formation was that? To which military unit did you belong and where did you work as a courier?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: After I was wounded, I became a courier.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: When they attacked Otes on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that as member of the BH army, you took part in the battle of Otes?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: No, I did not take part in the battle, I was defending Otes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What military unit was operational at the time and when did you take part in the combat regarding Otes in 1992?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: It was the 3rd Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the headquarters of the 3rd Motorised Brigade was locate, where was the command post of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't know at the time. Later on, as a courier, did you find out?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: In the industrial area, it was on Stup.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was it the electric distribution building?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if in 1992, when you took part in the combat and the fighting involving Otes, how were you dressed? Did you have any weapons? Did you wear a uniform? What kind of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Personally I did not carry any weapons because it was just a few rifles available, and if they knew that we were so well armed, they would have walked through Sarajevo. Maybe we had one rifle for 20 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When we talk about the battle for Otes, was there also the police of the army of BH, were there any special MUP units exist, any special commandment under Juka Prazina participating?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Do not go further from the subject that concerns us. I came to testify about the death of my wife about not the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trto, you told us that you were a courier in the BH army after you were wounded. So as of the month of December, 1992, can you tell us as such, what were your part -- what were you doing, what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I don't know how you know that I was a courier. Probably from this document. I was carrying mail. I did all the jobs linked to a job of a courier. I was heavily wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As a courier, therefore, as a soldier belonging to the BH army, did you distribute mail to military units?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: No. I was sort of a local courier. I was the internal, for the internal units. Could you please just ask me questions relating to the death of my wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trto, perhaps I should explain to you, if you have any difficulties in answering questions, would you please ask me to intervene and not start a debate with Defence counsel. I have to explain to you that you have been called by the Prosecution as we have heard because the Prosecution did want to put questions to you in relation to the death of your wife. On the other hand, being here as a witness, the Defence is entitled to ask you also questions about other subjects of course related to the situation, the war situation which existed at that time in Sarajevo. If you have any difficulties, please tell me but be aware that the Defence is also entitled to ask about what you know about the general circumstances. The accused has been charged with more than just the incident in which your wife died and you have been -- since you are now in this courtroom, you might have knowledge, information, which might be useful to the Defence as well. So I invite you to answer the questions of the Defence, and if you have any difficulties in doing so, please address me. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trto, in the course of examination-in-chief, you told my learned colleague from the Prosecution that you were a courier at the command of the BH army. Can you tell us where was the command post located? In other words, where is it that you went to work in the BH army command and what military formation was there that this was the command of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... said that he was working at the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague is following the transcript in English, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Perhaps there is a problem with the interpretation. On page 6, line 5, the witness said that he carried mail to the command so he had to work there because it was part of his job. So page 6, line 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... misrepresenting the evidence of the witness. Carrying mail to the headquarters is not the same as working at the headquarters. But perhaps you could rephrase your question, Ms. Pilipovic, and then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, as a courier, you carried mail to the command. Can you please tell us what command it was and where it was located.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: In 1993 - I don't know the exact month - it was transferred to the Dalekovod, which is located in the industrial area, and there was also a detached part of the command in another location, Valter Peric, and my route was from Valter Peric to the Dalekovod building.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, the Valter Peric building, in what street was it? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know because in peacetime I never went back to Stup, and I was there only in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you tell us that the Valter Peric building where the command was where you carried mail, that it was at Stup. That is as much as you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What military formation was located in the Valter Peric building?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were soldiers, ABiH soldiers, in the Valter Peric building, and if yes, what unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Probably the 3rd Motorised Brigade because it belonged to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us -- I believe that I did ask this question but I don't -- I am not sure whether I elicited the answer. How were members of the 3rd Motorised Brigade dressed?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I can't really remember. Later on, when the military was structured properly -- I am not really an expert in these military matters, but everybody wore some kind of uniform, the camouflage uniforms of sorts. Nobody was wearing civilian clothes or hardly anybody came to work in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trto, you confirmed that you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 18th of November, 1995. I will now quote a line from your statement on page 1. That would be page 2 of 0013544. When asked the question by my learned colleague, you stated that the incident happened on the 26th of September, 1993, that that is when your wife was killed. In your statement you said, "On about the 24th of September, 1993, I came back from the front line and my wife Edina told me that she wanted to visit her mother."

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Well, there is something wrong with that because I came home on the 26th of September, in the morning, and I sat down with my wife. We in the military were issued cigarettes, and since cigarettes cost 15 or 20 marks, we were trying to make do like everybody else, and sometimes I would give her half a pack of cigarettes and sometimes even more. Please, let me finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trto, did you state that you came back from the line?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: That is absurd because I was not on the line. After I was wounded, after the events at Otes, I never went to the line. I simply didn't want to risk my life to go somewhere like that. I didn't want to go any further away from the Valter Peric building.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain to us how come that in your statement that you gave to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor, it is stated that on around -- on about the 24th of September, 1993, you came back from the line? Did you in fact state that?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: No, I did not state that. I said that on the 26th of September, I had come home in the morning, gave my wife some cigarettes and spoke to her for a while, and then the phone rang. Perhaps this is --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trto, when you gave a statement to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor, in which language did you give your statement?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I gave it in my language, Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign a -- your statement in Serbian or in English?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Not in Serbian, in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign your statement in your mother tongue or in the English language?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I can't remember. Your Honour, could I we provided with this document so that I can see the documents we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's the document which been shown to you on which your signature appears. But if you would like to see it again. Mr. Usher, could you please assist. Do you speak or read any English, Mr. Trto?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can have the translation, too?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give the statement to the witness, both in the English language and in his mother tongue as specified by the witness. I have underlined this part so perhaps, Mr. Usher, if you could show this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot see anything that is underlined here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please read what is written there because we want to hear your words in the courtroom. We want to check whether what I have read to you is indeed correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the underlined part, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Please, could you just read what has been underlined here. If you can read it out loud, just this one line.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I read it, but I don't see my signature here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please read what is provided to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your signature is, as far as I understand, is on the English translation. This Chamber has not the statement in front of it, so if you please read just the line or the sentence which is underlined, aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: It is written here, "On the 24th of September, 1993, I came back from the line and my wife Edina." This is not correct. I never stated this and I never signed this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like Mr. Usher to give the statement back to me, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Trto, what you are saying is that the things that are stated in the statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor are not correct; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: On the 24th of September, I was not there. I said quite clearly that it was on the 26th. Maybe it was mistranslated, but I can tell you one thing, you don't -- in such occasions, you don't really know what you are saying and where you were. But I am telling you now, I was there sitting down with my wife on the 26th of September, and I just want to tell you, if I gave you a document in Chinese now --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I just want to make -- to let you know that you signed a statement in the English language where it says the 24th. So it's your signature there?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: It is possible that it is some kind of mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that you never said that this happened on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trto, can you please tell us, on that day when you were notified that your wife had been hit, had been shot, can you please tell us do you have any knowledge whether -- do you know whether the police attended the scene of the event?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I know that on on-site investigation was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After the police carried out the on-site investigation, did they also speak to you?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the contents of the official report drafted by the officers from the Novi Sarajevo police station?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: No. This is the first time that I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you looked at your wife when you identified her in the emergency ward premises. I think you said that she had two wounds.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think there were. But believe me, at that moment I was not really interested in how many wounds there were. The important thing was that she was no longer alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that this is really difficult for you, but you said that you looked at her and that you saw that there was a wound to her arm and also, if I remember correctly, you said that there was another wound?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I saw two wounds or, in fact, there was blood in two places. I saw also something on her side because she was lying there. I don't know whether it was on the left or on the right side. I can't remember any more. But you could see where the bullet had gone through her lungs. I didn't really look very closely. I just wanted to get out because I felt really bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know from what position fire was opened that day on the date when your wife was killed?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Well, that day, in the morning, there wasn't much shooting, much fighting going on. So when they went there, I spoke to my mother-in-law and she said that it was a quiet day. They met at the Cengic Vila, across a small bridge, and there was a small market there where people sold cigarettes and stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, from the point where your wife was killed, how far away from that point were the front lines? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I don't really know because I never measured it as you would say. But there is a part that is open between the two buildings. It is a parking lot. And the only place that has a line of sight to that area is Sanac. Now, this is what I heard, that their lines were at Sanac.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "Sanac," can you be more specific what part of the city is that? Is that Hrasno Grbavica, Hrasno Brdo?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I don't know exactly because, as children, we called it Sanac and that is what it is still called in Sarajevo. I don't know any other name. I do know, however, that it is above Hrasno, further up from Hrasno. If you look from Dolac Malta where the tramlines are going, it is not to the right, but to the left. It is above the transit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know or did you check at a later stage, you personally, whether the positions of the BH army and of the Republika Srpska army were there? Did you learn after the incident about that?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Well, no, I didn't learn that. But fire was opened all the time on the intersection at the Dolac Malta. I believe that the BH army was not there in that area where they would be able to operate because later on I went there and I stood there, waiting for them to shoot me, but they didn't open fire on me, because I just didn't care whether I would live or die.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you tell us that you went to that area, to that spot, which you said was the place from which fire was opened. What street was that?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: No, I did not go to the place from which fire was opened. I went to the place where my wife was killed. If you don't believe me, I will take you by the hand and lead you to that spot in Sarajevo

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, may I remind you that you took as much time and --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour. I just have a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how far way from that spot where you stood where your wife was killed to the other place?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Maybe 300, 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So how far away is it from that direction? You say it is 400 to 500 metres?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, thereabouts. It seems to be a mistake in translation. It isn't 300, but 400 to 500.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any positions of the BH army or Republika Srpska army there?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I don't know. I am not a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trto, in the course of the examination-in-chief, you were shown a document number 0026-9011. Could I please ask Mr. Usher to show the witness the document containing this page. There are two pages, 0026-9011 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is P1675.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 73, 75, thank you. No, 75, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trto, now I would like you to go to the statement that you signed. Do you see here this?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you confirm that the date is the 12th of December, 1994; can you confirm that? The 12th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you write this statement or did you just sign it?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I just signed it. I didn't write it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you tell us that you merely signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes, you can quite clearly see the difference in the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why did you go to the public security station or the police station and sign this statement there? Whose initiative was it?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I don't really remember. I simply can't remember. I don't remember any of it. After all, I am not a computer -- we had three years of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, we are not talking about the dates of the 24th of September 1993. We spoke about the 26th of September, 1993. Do you know whether in the period of the 24th, 25th and 26th that there were any conflicts between the BH army units and that the commander Musan Topalovic was killed, and that in those days and on those nights that the citizens of Sarajevo were exposed to fire opened by those military formations? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Your Honour. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At page 23, line 3, you made reference to, and I quote: "their lines at Sanac." When you say "their lines," what military force or forces were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Well, I have repeated this so many times and I will repeat it once again. This was not a religious war, nobody can tell me that. There were Serbs in Sarajevo. I know about Sarajevo but not for other towns. Sometimes you couldn't know what was happening in other buildings, but these people lived side by side with us. They went with us to fetch water. They were also being killed. I wanted to say "them." I didn't want to say Serbs because what do you call the people who lived side by side with us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand your feelings. I think Mr. Mundis would like to know when you talk about lines whether you want to refer to the lines of the armed forces of Republika Srpska or the armed forces of the Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I think that is what he wants to know, not what ethnicity these lines were held by. Yes.

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Well, of the army of Republika Srpska, that is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mundis

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if the Ozrenska Street is in the area of Sanac?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trto, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi would like to put a question to you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just a very brief question for you, sir. You said that your wife had been expelled from the place where she lived and that was in Grbavica, I believe, that your mother-in-law had actually been expelled. Who lived there?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: Well, it was a mixed composition, but the way she explained to me these people went down from Vrace and they simply deported all the non-Serbs, simply evicted them from their apartments and took away all their things and make them cross the river Miljacka, cross the bridge to Alija's state, they used to call it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trto -- yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, since a question was asked about the deportations of the Muslim population from Grbavica, my question, with your permission, would be whether the witness has any knowledge of any relocation -- not to use the term deportation, of the Serbian population from the parts of the city controlled by the BH army. I specifically mean the Sanac municipality. Does me know whether the Serbs left some parts of the towns to go to the areas controlled by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First I make an observation that the expulsion has been dealt with in examination-in-chief as well so you would have been able to ask that in cross-examination, but nevertheless I allow you to put this additional question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you have any knowledge of the Serbian population being expelled from the parts of the city controlled by the BH army and having to move to areas controlled by the Republika Srpska army? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: HABIB TRTO
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody was expelled in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Mr. Trto, this concludes your examination as a witness in this courtroom. Everyone understands that it brings back into your memory and testifying about the events such as you testified about is not easy. Nevertheless, I also hope that you understand that it is important for this Chamber to hear from those who were present at the relevant times at the relevant places, to hear their answers to the questions put to them by both Prosecution and by Defence and by the Judges. I thank you very much for coming and I wish you have a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please guide us through the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1673, official report police station Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, you would like to make an observation at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I may. In light of the fact that there was a missing page with respect to the translation and not withstanding the fact that there was no prejudice to the Defence, in light of the fact that they can read the document in its original language, the Prosecution will not seek to tender these two documents at this time, but would rather wait until a full translation is available for the benefit of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, another way of -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. I will reiterate the fact that we are hindered because your humble servant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis is saying that will not tender the document at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until some future time or future moment and that future moment, Mr. President, in order for you to be able to decide, is important for us to know that the Defence was hindered and handicapped and every day we have translations problems. Last night we received some documents that had absolutely nothing to do with the next witnesses. I am very tired of all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate what difficulties you had in cross-examining the witness on the second page which -- I am asking you what type of difficulties you had on the second page which contains a few entries handwritten and is apart from that a form? What difficulties did you face, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, I do not know since I do not have access to the translation of the document. In fact, this team is such a team that works together. We discuss a lot. We have ideas that come from our different backgrounds, and if I do not have access to technical documents in a language that they understand more or less, well, I must say I protest. If I cannot even protest when the Prosecution doesn't hand us -- doesn't give us some documents I will not do so. But it will not be the first time that I am asked to not say what I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Chamber is aware of the fact that apart from the entries appearing in it which appear at first sight Latin, rather than B/C/S, in which clearly indicates, I would say, the type of -- well, more or less the reasons of, that it has been translated after the witness read the first line of 16, that is what is the cause of death. And it -- these are medical terms that are there. Ms. Pilipovic is a native B/C/S speaker. We noticed that you are quite well able to read understand and speak B/C/S. So, therefore the Chamber wonders what extra information you would have if you had an English the translation and the Chamber also wonders in what way the absence of an English translation would have hindered you in cross-examining the witness. I am asking for specific problems you faced.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. Gladly. First of all, I must say that this form may contain some words that I do not know, linguistically. That is the first thing. And secondly, we have seen it but we have not said it, but this document seems to contain some handwriting and some typed areas. I don't know if some things are hidden and once again, we always ask for the production of original documents and I must say that there is some documents that I cannot read once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is a different issue. I ask you a specific question about translation. I would like you to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, gladly. This is what I read, Mr. President: [French phrase]. I cannot read what follows. Maybe there is an important translation. I don't know if the Court is able to read what follows. I cannot read what follows. It is a handwritten text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with all due respect to my learned colleagues, we have introduced numerous medical records here before and the translation unit will not translate the Latin phrases, into English at any rate. We can have this document translated for the courtesy of the Trial Chamber and that is what we are proposing to do. However, as you clearly indicated, the Defence team is quite capable of the reading this document in its original language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know if it is courtesy or an obligation to provide the Chamber. The Chamber knows that the Latin terms are never translated. I think Mr. Piletta-Zanin knows it. I think everyone knows it in this courtroom. That is clear. I think that is clear. That is enough argument on the admissibility of this document. We will give a decision after the break. The other documents, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1673.1 English translation; P1675, report of all sniper activities against the civilians in B/C/S; Exhibit P1675.1, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the report on sniper activity is admitted -- I am making a mistake. It is 1675, I will give a decision after the break and the other document was 1673 which is -- that is admitted. We will have a break until 10 minutes past 11.00. May I, before we actually have this break, make two short observations. It happens regularly that the Defence takes even a bit more time for the cross-examination than the Prosecution has take for examination-in-chief. I also noticed, and let's just take the example of today, that a lot of subjects were covered by the Defence which were not directly related to the examination-in-chief, and to some extent, they are allowed to do it. If, on the other hand, if you take every witness to the incident at the wedding party or whatever other subjects or to go through the -- if you take every witness to the issue of uniforms on which we had quite a lot of testimony and especially if there is no specific reason to assume that the witness would have specific knowledge on these issue, if you then at the end of the cross-examination might be faced with some time problems, I think it is up to the Defence to use the time as it wants to, but usually we, I think, if they do not want to take the risk, that they finally cannot put the questions in relation to the issues dealt with in examination-in-chief. It could be wise to start with those issues first. I would like to make one other observation. We have discussed before the matter of leading questions or not. I have explained to the Defence that there was no problem during cross-examination to ask questions in a leading way, even if these would be issues in dispute. At the same time, I would like to inform the Defence that in the tradition, where there is a difference between examination-in-chief and cross-examination, the rules are applicable and we do not apply these rules very strictly, but of course we orient ourselves to this rule, whenever you touch new ground, material, for the case of the Defence, issues that have not been dealt with in the examination-in-chief, that usually the questioning should be similar to an examination in chief. For example, I noticed today that on page 16, line 3 to 6, there were clear leading questions on issues that might very well in dispute. Since there was no objection, I didn't interfere but I would like to give this guidance to the Defence. My last request is to the technicians to do something about the clocks of our laptops, because according to the laptop, we have been in court already for three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, before the break, Mr. Mundis indicated that he would not tender Exhibit 1675, for reasons well known, that is that one page was not translated. So therefore we don't have to decide on the admissibility. Nevertheless, the Chamber orders the Prosecution, because we find it evidence that might well be relevant, we order the Prosecution to provide the Chamber this documents with a full and proper translation within one week from now on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That will be done. Mr. President, before we call the next witness, yesterday, I asked for an indication as to the period of time for the cross-examination of Mr. Donia. I received a letter faxed late last night from the Defence, requesting copies of some further material in relation to Donia but I haven't yet received any indication as to how long the cross-examination is proposed to be as far as the Defence is concerned. I would be grateful for that. The latest information I have in relation to Mr. Donia is that he is required to give evidence in another case as well in the next two weeks. It now looks as if that evidence will be the week after next, that is, from the 22nd of April. I, therefore, have in mind to call him on the morning of Thursday, the 17th, I think it is, of April. That would leave a maximum of two days of cross-examination. I don't suggest that he would require two days of cross-examination, but that is what is available at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, can you inform the Chamber about the time you should need.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It should be the 18th of April. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, certainly. The Defence, unfortunately, has no indication to give you with regards to the time that we will need. We are terribly sorry and we apologise ahead of time because we do not know how long it will take us. It is a very important witness to our mind, and I believe that the time will be longer than what the Prosecution indicated. If the Defence is not able to say so, it is because we have asked the Prosecution to receive all the documents that are -- that figure in this quasi-expert witness report for the following reason: It is a 24-page document. There are 14 pages of text and 10 pages sent us to various different documents. This is why we wanted to obtain all this reference material and read what we can. Therefore, we will only then be able to tell you how long we will need to cross-examine this witness. But according to what we foresee, it is probably much longer period of time than what the Prosecution has proposed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much documents are still missing? Mr. Ierace, could you tell us, I mean, is there 95 per cent or 65 per cent or 25 per cent of the attached documents disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, when we disclosed the report on the 14th of February, which I think is 14 pages long, we disclosed it with it two large binders full of the material which Mr. Donia referred to his report. So I would be surprised if there is any documentation mentioned in his report which has not been provided to the Defence. The only other matter is this: We have also provided tapes, disclosed tapes to the Defence of evidence given by Mr. Donia in past proceedings. I think that there have been five altogether. There is still one tape to come, which we're told by the translation unit should be available today. So at this stage I am not aware of any outstanding material. Mr. Piletta-Zanin in his letter, sent to me in French, referred to two documents in particular. I am having the material brought into the Trial Chamber this morning, to check whether in fact those two documents were in the two folders. I'm sorry, it is the Registry which is providing the tapes, not the translation unit, and we are told by the Registry that the remaining tape should be available today. Thank you. Mr. President, those two documents have just arrived. So if you could allow me just a minute, I'll check to see if the two documents indicated by the Defence are, in fact, in those two volumes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you, Mr. Ierace, whether you feel that the Prosecution was under an obligation to provide the tapes of the testimony of Mr. Donia in other cases or was it, in your view at least, a matter of assisting the Defence or were you under an obligation, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I understand it, there is no strict obligation on the Prosecution to do that. It is something that we do as a matter of courtesy, if you like, as part of disclosure of all material in our possession which touches upon that witness. More specifically, of course, Mr. Donia's report concerns the recent history of Sarajevo. It is, as far as the reports go, a very brief one. The material within the tapes, of course, deals with other parts of the former Yugoslavia and other periods of time, so I don't see that tape as in any way hindering the Defence's cross-examination. It would save time perhaps if the Defence could indicate the title of those two documents that they are particularly concerned about. I apologise for interrupting my friend. I only rise to my feet in the interests of saving time. The relevant sentence from the letter as translated into English is to the effect that the Defence needs access to text referring to number 3233 and 3199. Perhaps my friend could indicate whether that is a footnote from a report or numbers in the index to the two volumes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. President. The Defence thought that we were quite clear. We wish to obtain the following. With regards to -- we have a report. Half of these -- the indications in the report send us to various sources, so I believe that there is more than 100 footnotes. The ERN documents as part of these footnotes and some of them are not, but those ERN numbers are with the Prosecution and we would like to obtain them. I am asking this because we know that search engines that were handed us so courteously by the Prosecution do not work well enough and we cannot find these documents. We are wasting a great deal of time, whereas the Prosecution has today within their possession a better search engine, and we would like them to hand us a hard copy which seems to be actually an obligation, given the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. nature of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it seems like this is going to take some time. There are about 100 footnotes to the report. Those numbers clearly could not relate to the footnotes. The indexes to the two volumes refer to footnote numbers, so again it is not easy to understand what my friend means when he refers to four-digit numbers because, of course, that doesn't relate to the ERNs either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We just only received copies of the correspondence which deal with the -- we, of course, the Chamber, the report of Mr. Donia has been filed and so the Chamber is also in a position to see whether we are talking about one-tenth of a per cent which might be missing or whether there is a serious handicap for the Defence. If necessary, I will given an opportunity later on for further debate, but I will strictly limit it in time. We also see whether the failing documents are such that the Defence is handicapped to given an estimate of the time they would need for cross-examination. There is a practical problem because the Prosecution has to schedule the arrangements for Mr. Donia. So the Chamber will have a serious look at whether the missing documents are such that it would prevent the Defence to give an estimate of time they would need and the Chamber asks to reconsider -- asks the Defence to reconsider whether they could come up with an estimate, although some pages are missing. I think for very practical reasons, the witness is waiting outside and as far as I know there are some physical hindrances as well, so that is the reason why I do not want to continue this debate at this very moment. I think the witness had waited perhaps already a bit too long. Mr. Usher, could you please bring the witness into the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the usher leaves the courtroom, I wanted to make sure, is the following witness Mr. Enver?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. I have a witness on my list who is a protected witness. I am not dealing with any names, therefore. I have Witness AJ on my list. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a coordination problem. We just have to look at our list. Excuse us one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please be seated, but don't yet put on the earphones. Mr. Usher, could you please put on the earphones for just one second so that...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. We have now found this witness on our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution has sought protective measures for you, and they are granted. That means that no one in the outside world can see your face and that no one in this courtroom will use your real name. Please keep that in mind as well while testifying, because you might easily refer to a place or to a person which might make it possible for other people to identify you. Before you give testimony in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. So Mrs. AJ, as we will call you, would you please make that declaration and the text will be handed out to you now by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown P3679. Madam, is your name correctly stated on that piece of paper in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is your date of birth also correctly stated on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might that be returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, I will have to leave the courtroom for a few minutes just to make a quick phone call, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might I just clarify that the microphone be turned off at the end of each question

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear you. I didn't hear. Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify whether I have to turn the microphone off after I ask each question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we have no voice distortion so...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Madam, have you lived in Sarajevo since 1979?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you married and do you have two children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are both children female?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: During the armed conflict in Sarajevo, were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the date on which you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: On the 7th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What day of the week was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: It was a Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The previous day Friday, the 6th of November, had you been working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes. I was subject to the work obligation so I went to work. After the office hours I went to the park, which is in the immediate vicinity of the company of where I worked, to gather some twigs, because I wanted to find an oven fueled by solid fuel because I wanted to bake some bread and there was no power, no electricity, no gas and this was the only way we could do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I do not want to know where you worked or what you did at work but request you answer this question: Did your work have anything to do with the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In terms of where you lived, was it a house or an apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: It was an apartment building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How many floors did the apartment building have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Eighteen. I lived on the sixth floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So on the Friday, the 6th of November, you gathered some wood from a park --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: It was on the 7th of November -- no, I am sorry. You are absolutely correct. It was on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You gathered some wood in a park in order to make a fire is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was that a fire to do some cooking or a fire to keep warm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: For cooking. That was our primary concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The following day Saturday, the 7th of November, did you go somewhere with the wood that you collected the day before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: Yes. I carried the wood and the bread to a neighbour of mine, to bake it, because I did not have a wood oven, wood-powered oven.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Did you go with someone, and if you did, please do not tell us the name of that person.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I went there with a neighbour of mine because she also wanted to bake some bread. Because in our apartment building, none of us had a wood oven so we had to go to a neighbour of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. What was the time approximately that you left your apartment to go to the other place to bake some bread?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: I can't say with any precision, but perhaps around half past 2.00 or around 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the weather like at that stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AJ
utterances.text: The weather was quite unusual for that time of year because it was sunny and quite warm. That November was quite warm.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember what sort of clothes you were wearing that day?
